mkt-01.title: Markets and Customer Value
explain: **Marketing** is the work of creating, communicating, and delivering something of value to customers so that a mutually beneficial **exchange** takes place. People often use the word as a synonym for advertising or selling, but advertising and selling are only parts of marketing. Everything from deciding what to make to the relationship after the sale is marketing.

Marketing starts in people's minds. Let us distinguish three words.
- **Need**: a lack that a person feels in living. Example: hunger, having to get somewhere.
- **Want**: a wish for a specific way of satisfying a need. Example: wanting to eat freshly baked bread.
- **Demand**: the wants that a person is actually able and willing to pay for. If someone has no money or no intention to buy, the want exists but it is not demand.

A **market** is a group of people who are able and willing to buy a certain product. Note that it is a set of people, not a place. Marketers first look at what the people in a market want, and then bring out a product that fits.

Customers buy **value** rather than the product itself. Value is the feeling that comes from comparing what the customer **gets** with what the customer **gives up**. What they get includes taste, convenience, and mood; what they give up includes not only money but also time and effort. Even if the price is low, value can feel low if the customer has to travel far and wait long.

mkt-02.title: Segmentation, Targeting, Positioning
explain: No product pleases everyone. So marketers divide the market, choose which part to aim at, and decide what image they will leave in those people's minds. These three steps are commonly called **STP**.

1. **Segmentation**: divide the market into groups of similar people.
2. **Targeting**: choose the segment to focus on among those divided.
3. **Positioning**: set a place in the target customers' minds that distinguishes the product from competing products.

There are four commonly used bases for segmentation.
- **Geographic**: region of residence, city size.
- **Demographic**: age, gender, household type, income.
- **Psychographic**: lifestyle, values, tastes.
- **Behavioral**: purchase frequency, usage occasion, benefits sought.

**Positioning** is less a matter of how the product was actually made than of how customers **perceive** it. A diagram that uses two criteria as axes and plots competing products as points is called a **positioning map**. Points that are close together mean that customers see the products as similar.

An empty spot on the map looks like an opportunity, but whether enough customers want that spot must be checked separately. Being empty is only the fact that nobody has entered; it is not evidence that demand exists.

mkt-03.title: The Marketing Mix: The 4Ps
explain:
Once the target customers are set, specific means of delivering value to them are put together. The combination of these means is called the **marketing mix**, and it is commonly divided into four Ps.
- **Product**: what is sold. Quality, design, assortment, service.
- **Price**: how much is charged. List price, discounts, payment terms.
- **Place**: where and through what channel it is sold. Store location, online, delivery.
- **Promotion**: how it is communicated and persuaded. Advertising, social media, events, word of mouth.

The four must not operate separately. If a business projects a luxurious image but sets very low prices and sells anywhere at all, customers cannot tell what kind of shop it is. When the four point in the same direction, a consistent message reaches the target customers.

Price is set by looking at many factors, but the basic calculation is simple.
- **Profit** = (selling price − cost) × quantity sold
- **Discounted price** = list price × (100 − discount rate) / 100
Cost is the expense of making or bringing in one item. This calculation is the simplest model; real shops also have other costs such as rent and labor.

mkt-04.title: The Consumer's Purchase Decision Process
explain:
When people buy something, they usually go through several stages. The most widely used simple model has five stages.
1. **Problem recognition**: the person feels that something is lacking.
2. **Information search**: the person looks up reviews, what acquaintances say, and shop information.
3. **Evaluation of alternatives**: the person compares candidates against criteria.
4. **Purchase**: the person picks one and pays.
5. **Post-purchase evaluation**: the person compares the result with expectations and feels satisfied or dissatisfied.
Real people do not always follow this order exactly. They may skip stages or change the order. This model is not a law of reality but a framework for organizing thought.

The length of the process varies with how important the item to be bought is. An item that is expensive or whose failure would be a burden is a **high-involvement** purchase, and people compare for a long time. An item that is cheap and bought often is a **low-involvement** purchase, and people often choose by habit.

The last stage matters too. Satisfaction after purchase leads to buying again and to word of mouth to those around, and dissatisfaction leads the opposite way. That is why post-purchase evaluation is drawn in the figure as an arrow that loops back to the next purchase.

mkt-05.title: Brands
explain: A **brand** is a term covering the name and symbols that distinguish a product or shop from others, together with the image and expectations they create in customers' minds. A logo is only the visible part of a brand. Even with the same logo, if the experience is bad, the brand's image gets worse.

A brand can usually be thought of in three layers.
- **Actual experience**: whether the product, service, and handling follow through as promised.
- **Name and symbols**: marks such as the name, logo, colors, and tone of voice.
- **Mental associations**: the image and expectations customers recall from that name.

There are a few concepts often used when talking about the strength of a brand.
- **Awareness**: the degree to which the name is known or can be recalled.
- **Image**: the associations attached to the name (for example, trustworthy, warm).
- **Loyalty**: the degree to which people keep choosing it even when other alternatives exist.

The advantage of a brand is that it reduces the effort customers spend choosing, because they can guess from the name alone what the experience will be. In return, if the promise and the experience diverge, trust can be cut down all at once, so consistency matters.

The repurchase rate is a simple number for roughly estimating loyalty. **Repurchase rate** = number of customers who bought again / number of first-time customers × 100 (%). This number varies with the period and definition, so the same standard must be used when comparing.

mkt-06.title: Marketing Research and Ethics
explain:
Marketing decisions are better based on data than on guesses. **Marketing research** is the work of collecting and interpreting data about customers and the market. Data is divided into two kinds.
- **Primary data**: data collected directly for a given purpose. Surveys, interviews, observation, experiments.
- **Secondary data**: data that someone has already collected. Statistical data, sales records, public reports.

To trust research results, the **sample** is important. A sample is the part of the whole that was actually studied. If the sample is skewed to one side, the result is skewed too. For example, if satisfaction is asked only of regular customers, the result 'all customers are satisfied' is likely to come out. This problem is called **sample bias**.

The most common mistake in reading research results is to read **correlation** as **causation**. Correlation is two values rising and falling together, and causation is one causing the other. Even if they appear to move together, there may be a third factor moving both. To confirm causation, a more rigorous method such as an experiment with controlled conditions is needed.

Ethics also accompanies marketing. Advertising that invites misunderstanding is a typical problem.
- '#1' or 'the best' with no stated basis.
- Conditions hidden in small print.
- Picking out only some results to make them look like the whole.
What is legally permitted differs by country and situation, and it is not an area this course can judge. Still, it is clear that making customers misunderstand the facts may sell in the short term but loses trust.

mkt-07.title: Involvement and the Elaboration Likelihood Model (ELM)
explain: Seeing the same advertisement, one person reads the product description carefully while another remembers only the background music and the model. This is because the depth at which messages are processed differs from person to person and situation to situation. The key concept explaining this difference is **involvement**, and the persuasion theory built on it is the **Elaboration Likelihood Model** (ELM).

**Involvement** is the degree to which a product or purchase decision is important and relevant to the consumer personally. Purchases that are expensive, risky, and related to the self, such as a house or a car, are often high involvement, while cheap and repetitive purchases such as gum or tissue are often low involvement. High-involvement consumers actively seek and compare information, while low-involvement consumers decide by habit or simple cues.

explain.alt: Flow diagram of the Elaboration Likelihood Model. From "Persuasive message" it leads to "Are motivation and ability sufficient?" If "Yes," it goes to "Central route: weighing the quality of arguments" then "Lasting attitude change"; if "No," it goes to "Peripheral route: cues such as model and music" then "Temporary attitude change."

explain: According to ELM, there are two routes of persuasion. When **motivation** (involvement) and **ability** (knowledge, time, concentration) to process the message are sufficient, it is processed by the **central route**. The person weighs the quality of the arguments (performance data, evidence), and if persuaded by good arguments, the attitude change is **lasting** and likely to lead to behavior. When motivation or ability is lacking, the message is processed by the **peripheral route**. **Peripheral cues** such as an attractive model, a celebrity, music, and the length of the message influence the judgment, and the attitude change is **temporary**.

Marketing implications: use specific evidence and comparison data for high-involvement targets, and memorable cues and repeated exposure for low-involvement targets. Even for the same product, involvement changes with the situation. Bottled water, usually low involvement, can become high involvement when choosing water for a baby. Also, the same element works differently depending on the route. An athlete as a model can be an **argument** (expertise) for a sports drink or a mere **cue** (likability).

Limitations: actual processing does not divide neatly into two routes but lies on a continuum, and the two routes sometimes operate at the same time. Involvement is hard to observe directly, so research design is important. Persuasion techniques must also be used within limits that do not mislead consumers, and exaggerated advertising is restricted by law and ethics (Stage 1, marketing ethics).

mkt-08.title: The Multiattribute Attitude Model and Reference Groups
explain: Why does a consumer like brand B more than brand A? The tool that breaks vague "liking" into elements a marketer can analyze and change is the **multiattribute attitude model**. And that attitude is not formed alone. Family, friends, and admired groups, that is, **reference groups**, have a large influence. (English summary of the formula paragraph below: Fishbein's multiattribute attitude model treats the attitude toward a brand, A_o, as the weighted sum over attributes i of the belief strength b_i (the belief that the brand has attribute i) times the evaluation e_i (the importance of attribute i). With standardized importance weights w_i that sum to 1, brands can be compared by the sum of w_i times b_i.)

피시바인의 다속성 태도 모형은 브랜드에 대한 태도를 속성별 평가의 가중합으로 본다. $$A_o = \sum_{i} b_i \times e_i$$ $b_i$는 그 브랜드가 속성 $i$를 갖추었다는 **믿음**의 강도, $e_i$는 속성 $i$에 대한 **평가**(중요도)다. 표준화된 중요도 가중치 $w_i$(합 1)를 쓰면 $\sum w_ib_i$로 점수를 비교할 수 있다.

explain: This model shows concretely the strategies for changing attitudes. (1) **Change beliefs**: present evidence that "our battery lasts longer than you think" (raising beliefs about one's own brand). (2) **Change importance**: persuade that the attribute where one is strong (battery) is more important. (3) **Add a new attribute**: highlight an attribute not yet considered (ease of repair). (4) **Change beliefs about competitors** (comparative advertising; beware of legal limits).

A **reference group** is a group that an individual takes as a standard for attitudes and behavior. There are **membership groups** the person directly belongs to (family, colleagues), **aspirational groups** the person wants to belong to, and **dissociative groups** the person wants to keep distance from. Reference groups exert influence in three ways. **Informational influence** (trusting what experts or experienced people say), **utilitarian influence** (conforming to gain approval or avoid criticism), and **value-expressive influence** (conforming to resemble an admired group). The influence is especially large for **products seen by others** (clothes, cars) and for **luxury goods**.

Limitations: the multiattribute model assumes that consumers calculate attribute by attribute, but in reality **noncompensatory** decisions are also common, in which an attribute that falls short of a threshold leads to immediate elimination (for example, if the price exceeds the budget, the product is excluded regardless of other strengths). Also, even a good attitude may not lead to purchase because of price, stock, or circumstances (the attitude-behavior gap).

mkt-09.title: Prospect Theory and Price Perception
explain: Giving a 100,000-won product a "20,000-won discount" and setting its list price at "80,000 won" yield the same price, yet consumers react differently. This is because consumers judge price not as an absolute amount but **by comparing it to a reference point**. Kahneman and Tversky's **prospect theory** explains this way of judging and has direct implications for pricing strategy.

explain.alt: The value function of prospect theory. The horizontal axis shows gains (right) and losses (left) from the reference point, and the vertical axis is psychological value. A curve passing through the reference point rises gently on the gain side and falls more steeply on the loss side. The labels read "Gain side: increases gently" and "Loss side: decreases steeply."

explain: Three key points of prospect theory: (1) **Reference dependence**: people judge value not by the final state but by the **change** (gain or loss) from a reference point. (2) **Loss aversion**: for the same size, a loss feels much larger than a gain (roughly twice as large). This is why the curve is steeper on the loss side in the figure. (3) **Diminishing sensitivity**: the farther from the reference point, the less the same change is felt. A gain of 10,000 won from 0 won and a gain of 10,000 won from 1,000,000 won to 1,010,000 won are the same 10,000 won, but the former feels larger.

**Reference price** in price perception: consumers compare with a price in their mind (the price paid last time, the list price, the price of a competing product). A discount display that shows the list price together raises the reference price and makes the consumer feel a "gain." Conversely, a price increase is a "loss" relative to the reference price, so resistance is strong. That is why, even for the same rate of increase, less noticeable methods are used, such as reducing the package size (shrinkflation) or reducing discounts, which raises issues of consumer trust and ethics.

Pricing tactics that come from prospect theory: **segregate gains and integrate losses.** Benefits are split into several and shown separately (basic discount + free gift + free shipping), while costs are bundled into one (a package that includes option prices). Also, **free** (0 won) is a special reference point, so the difference between 1 won and 0 won is perceived as far larger than the mathematical difference. **Decoy effect**: adding a third option that people will not choose makes the target option look relatively attractive.

Limits and ethics: the size of loss aversion differs by person and situation, and some studies find it weakens among experienced traders. Also, displaying a false list price that artificially manipulates the reference point (showing as the discount basis a high list price at which the item was never actually sold) misleads consumers and can be subject to legal regulation. This lesson deals with principles of consumer psychology and is not practical pricing advice.

examples.title: Segregating Gains

Interpretation: Because of diminishing sensitivity, when gains are shown separately, each gain is evaluated in the steep region near the reference point, so the total perceived value is larger. (b) tends to feel more attractive.

mkt-10.title: Positioning Maps and Competitive Advantage
explain: In Stage 1 we saw the basics of STP (segmentation, targeting, positioning). Positioning is occupying a place that distinguishes a product from competing products **in the minds of target customers**. This lesson covers how to find and hold that place systematically.

A **positioning map** (perceptual map) is a diagram that uses two dimensions that consumers consider important as axes and plots as points **how several brands are perceived** by consumers. The axes are chosen through consumer research. The map reveals areas of fierce competition and empty areas. But an empty area is not always an opportunity. One must also check **whether enough customers want that spot** (ideal point analysis). It may be empty because nobody wants it.

Key elements of positioning: (1) **Frame of reference**: which category of products it competes with (is it an energy drink, or a coffee substitute?). (2) **Points of parity** (POP): the basic conditions that must be met to belong to that category. (3) **Points of difference** (POD): distinctive associations meaningful to customers that customers believe make the brand superior to competitors. A point of difference must be **desirable** to customers, **feasible** for the company, and **distinct** from competitors.

Positioning is linked to types of competitive advantage. As in generic strategies in management, there are **cost advantage** (the same value more cheaply) and **differentiation** (higher value at a higher price). In marketing these are expressed as value propositions: "more for more," "the same for less," "less for much less," and so on. The danger is **positioning confusion**, promising "everything to every customer."

**Repositioning**: when the market changes or the existing position loses its appeal, the position is moved. But changing a perception already formed takes much time and money and risks losing existing customers. Limitations: a positioning map shows only two dimensions, so it simplifies complex competition. Also, perceptions differ with the research sample and the questions, so the results should not be trusted blindly.

mkt-11.title: Brand Equity and Brand Extension
explain: Even for products of the same quality made in the same factory, the price consumers are willing to pay differs depending on which brand is attached. This difference created by the brand name is **brand equity**. If Stage 1 covered the basics of brands, this lesson covers how brand equity is built and how it is leveraged (extended).

In Keller's **customer-based brand equity** (CBBE) view, brand equity is "the differential effect that brand knowledge has on customer response to marketing activity." Even with the same advertising and the same price, customers respond more favorably to a strong brand. Its sources are **brand awareness** (how easily it comes to mind: recognition and recall) and **brand image** (which associations come to mind: their strength, favorability, and uniqueness).

The CBBE pyramid shows the stages of brand building. (1) **Salience** (the brand is known and linked to a category) → (2) **performance** (function) and **imagery** (social and psychological associations) → (3) customer **judgments** (quality, credibility) and **feelings** (warmth, fun) → (4) **resonance** (loyalty, attachment, community, active engagement). The lower stages must be solid to climb higher.

**Brand extension** is using an existing brand name on a new product. There are new flavors and sizes within the same category (**line extension**) and moves into other categories (**category extension**). Advantages: it quickly gains awareness and trust for the new product and reduces marketing costs. The key to success is **fit**. The core associations of the parent brand must also be meaningful in the new category (a camera brand with a precision-technology image → medical imaging devices). When fit is low, consumers feel confused, and if the extension fails, even the parent brand's image can be damaged (**dilution**).

Measuring brand equity: the difference in evaluation of the same product with the brand hidden and revealed, the difference in willingness-to-pay price (price premium), awareness and association surveys, repurchase rate, and so on. Limitations: brand equity is intangible, so results differ greatly depending on the measurement method, and it does not show up well in short-term sales metrics. Excessive discounting may raise short-term sales but erode long-term brand equity.

mkt-12.title: Value-Based Pricing and Price Elasticity
explain: Of the marketing mix, price is the only element that **generates revenue**, and it is also the element that can be changed most quickly. There are broadly three ways to set a price: **cost-based**, which adds a profit margin to cost; **competition-based**, which takes competitors' prices as the standard; and **value-based**, which takes the value the customer perceives as the standard. This lesson covers value-based pricing and the **price elasticity** needed to judge it.

Cost-based prices are easy to calculate but ignore how much customers are willing to pay. If customers are willing to pay much more, money is left on the table, and if cost is higher than customer value, the product will not sell no matter how much margin is added. **Value-based pricing** starts from the value customers get, sets the price from that, and designs cost to fit that price.

A method often used for industrial goods is **economic value to the customer** (EVC). The price of the alternative the customer currently uses (**reference value**) plus the extra value our product gives over the alternative (**differentiation value**: cost savings, performance gains) is the maximum price the customer can pay. $$EVC = \text{준거가치} + \text{차별화 가치}$$ (Here 준거가치 is the reference value and 차별화 가치 is the differentiation value.) The actual price is set below EVC to leave the customer an incentive to buy. The difference between price and EVC is the customer's gain, and the difference between price and cost is the company's gain.

**Price elasticity** shows how sensitive demand is to a change in price (in the formula, 수요량 변화율 is the percentage change in quantity demanded and 가격 변화율 is the percentage change in price). $$E = \frac{\text{수요량 변화율}}{\text{가격 변화율}}$$ If the absolute value is greater than 1, demand is **elastic** (lowering the price increases sales revenue); if less than 1, it is **inelastic** (raising the price increases sales revenue). Demand is more elastic the more substitutes there are, the larger the share of income the good takes up, and the less it is a necessity.

Limits and cautions: elasticity differs by price range and time, and short-run and long-run responses differ. Even if revenue rises, profit may not (cost must be considered). Also, changing prices often makes consumers wait for discounts, and price discrimination can raise fairness controversies. Colluding with competitors on prices is illegal. This lesson deals with principles and is not practical pricing advice.

examples.title: Calculating EVC
body: Conditions (hypothetical): The existing cutting tool a factory uses costs 500,000 won (used for one year). The new tool has the same lifespan and saves 300,000 won a year in labor by shortening replacement work time.
Step 1: $EVC = 50 + 30 = 80$ (in units of 10,000 won).

Step 2: If the price is set at 650,000 won, the customer gains 150,000 won, and if the cost is 400,000 won, the company gains 250,000 won. If the cost-based price "cost + 25% = 500,000 won" had been applied, 150,000 won would have been left on the table.

mkt-13.title: Distribution Channel Design and Double Marginalization
explain: Even a good product sells only if it is where customers can buy it. The path a product takes from the manufacturer to the consumer is the **distribution channel**. Why are **intermediaries** such as wholesalers, retailers, and online platforms needed, and what problems arise when a channel gets longer?

Intermediaries exist because they **reduce the number of transactions** and specialize functions. If 5 manufacturers and 5 consumers deal directly, 25 transactions are needed, but with one intermediary only 10 are needed. Intermediaries perform functions such as assortment (many manufacturers' products in one place), storage, transport, selling in small quantities, providing information, and extending credit. Even if intermediaries are eliminated, **the functions do not disappear**; someone else must perform them.

Channel design decisions: **channel length** (direct selling vs. going through wholesalers and retailers) and **channel breadth** (intensive distribution: as many outlets as possible / selective distribution: a chosen few / exclusive distribution: one outlet per territory). Convenience goods are often intensively distributed, and luxury goods exclusively. Differences in goals easily cause **conflict** among channel members (direct online sales eat into dealers' sales), and coordinating this is channel management.

The **double marginalization** problem: if the manufacturer and the retailer each independently maximize their own profit, the manufacturer adds a margin to the wholesale price and the retailer adds another margin on top of it. As a result the final consumer price is higher, sales volume falls, and **the two firms' combined profit** is also smaller than when a single integrated firm sets the price. In linear demand $Q = a - bP$, this can be confirmed by comparing the integrated firm's optimal price with the retail price in the separated case.

Solutions to double marginalization are cooperative devices such as **vertical integration** (one firm does both), **quantity discounts and two-part tariffs** (lowering the wholesale price and charging a fixed fee), **revenue-sharing contracts**, and **suggested retail prices**. Limitation: forcibly fixing resale prices is subject to competition law in many countries. This lesson deals with principles and is not distribution contract or legal advice.

examples.title: Calculating Double Marginalization
body: Conditions (hypothetical): demand $Q = 100 - P$, unit manufacturing cost 20.
Step 1 (integrated): maximize profit $(P - 20)(100 - P)$ → $P = 60$, $Q = 40$, profit 1,600.

Step 2 (separated): at wholesale price $w$ the retailer maximizes $(P - w)(100 - P)$ → $P = (100 + w)/2$, $Q = (100 - w)/2$. The manufacturer maximizes $(w - 20)(100 - w)/2$ → $w = 60$. Then $P = 80$, $Q = 20$, manufacturer profit 800, retailer profit 400, total 1,200. Compared with integration, the price is higher and sales volume and total profit are lower.

Step 1: Direct dealing takes $4 \times 6 = 24$ transactions.
Step 2: Going through one wholesaler takes $4 + 6 = 10$. With fewer transactions, total distribution cost can fall.

mkt-14.title: Omnichannel and the Customer Journey
explain: A consumer searches for a product on a mobile phone, touches it in person at a store, goes home and orders online, and picks it up at the store. Several channels are intertwined in a single purchase. The focus of marketing is shifting from **multichannel**, in which channels were run separately, to **omnichannel**, which integrates them so that customers have a seamless experience in any channel.

**Multichannel** runs several channels but manages each separately. The online price and the store price differ, the online shopping cart cannot be seen in the store, and something bought online cannot be returned in the store. **Omnichannel** integrates inventory, customer information, prices, and promotions so that, from the customer's point of view, it is experienced as "one brand." Examples: pickup in store after an online order, checking store inventory online, the same membership benefits in every channel.

A tool for designing omnichannel is the **customer journey map**. It draws, in time order, all the **touchpoints** (advertising, search, store, app, delivery, customer service) that the customer meets in the process from awareness → exploration → purchase → use → repurchase and recommendation, and finds the customer's emotions and **pain points** at each touchpoint. Improvement starts with the biggest pain point.

Phenomena of the omnichannel era: **showrooming** (looking in the store and buying cheaper online) and **webrooming** (researching online and buying in the store). Showrooming creates the problem of leaving only the store's operating costs, but omnichannel firms turn cannibalization between channels into an opportunity by steering customers who looked in the store to buy on their own online channel. For this, organization and compensation must also change, for example by evaluating store staff's performance not by "store sales" but by "total all-channel sales of their assigned customers."

Limitations: omnichannel integration requires large investment in integrating inventory and information systems, and attributing performance across channels (which channel made the sale?) is difficult and causes internal conflict. Also, integrating customer information across channels requires observing privacy principles (stated purpose, consent, minimal collection). This lesson is conceptual and is not advice on building practical systems.

examples.title: Pain Points in a Customer Journey
body: Conditions (hypothetical): A customer journey survey at a furniture company. Awareness (advertising, satisfied) → exploration (website, satisfied) → store visit (satisfied) → no delivery schedule notice after ordering (major dissatisfaction) → hard-to-follow assembly instructions (dissatisfaction).

mkt-15.title: Integrated Marketing Communications (IMC) and Measuring Advertising Effects
explain: Consumers encounter a brand's messages through TV ads, search ads, social media, store displays, promotional events, news articles, and recommendations from acquaintances. If these messages say different things, the brand image blurs. **Integrated marketing communications** (IMC) is an approach that coordinates all communication means so that they deliver **one consistent message**.

The communication mix: **advertising** (paid, mass reach), **sales promotion** (coupons, discounts, and samples that induce short-term purchase), **PR** (building trust through press coverage and events), **personal selling** (direct consultation, suited to complex products), and **digital and direct marketing** (personalized messages, easy to measure response). Each means has different strengths, so they are deployed to match the stage of the customer journey: advertising and PR at the awareness stage, content and comparison information at the consideration stage, and promotion and personal selling at the purchase stage.

Basic metrics of advertising exposure: **Reach**: the percentage of the target customers who saw the ad at least once. **Frequency**: on average how many times those who saw the ad saw it. **GRP** (gross rating points; in the formula, 도달률 is reach and 평균 빈도 is average frequency): $$GRP = \text{도달률(\%)} \times \text{평균 빈도}$$ With a reach of 60% and an average frequency of 3, the GRP is 180. Even at the same GRP, whether to go wide and shallow (high reach, low frequency) or narrow and deep depends on the goal. Reach matters for awareness of a new brand, and frequency matters for understanding a complex message.

**Cost efficiency**: CPM (cost per 1,000 impressions; 광고비 is advertising cost and 노출 수 is the number of impressions) $= \frac{\text{광고비}}{\text{노출 수}} \times 1000$. In digital advertising, cost per click (CPC) and cost per acquisition (CPA) are also used. But having many **intermediate metrics** such as impressions or clicks does not guarantee that sales rose. Whether advertising actually increased sales (causal effect) is checked with the next stage's A/B tests or regional experiments.

Limitations: if frequency is too high, **ad fatigue** reduces the effect or creates resentment. How to credit a purchase influenced by several channels together (**attribution**) is a problem with no single right answer. A "last click" rule underestimates the contribution of awareness-stage advertising. This lesson is conceptual and is not advice on running actual advertising. Advertising must comply with laws on labeling and advertising.

mkt-16.title: Customer Lifetime Value (CLV) and Retention
explain: If acquiring one new customer costs 50,000 won, is that customer worth it? Looking only at the profit from a single purchase, perhaps not, but if the customer buys repeatedly for several years, the story changes. **Customer lifetime value** (CLV) is the present value of the profit a customer will bring to the company while the relationship lasts. It is the key metric that makes one see marketing as an **investment** rather than a cost. (English summary of the formula paragraph below: if a customer leaves an annual contribution margin m, the retention rate is a constant r, and the discount rate is d, then CLV = m × (1 + d)/(1 + d − r), assuming the first year's profit is received at the start of the year. Ignoring discounting (d = 0), CLV = m/(1 − r), and 1/(1 − r) is the expected relationship duration; with a retention rate of 80%, the relationship lasts 5 years on average.)

단순화한 CLV 공식: 고객 한 명이 매년 공헌이익 $m$을 남기고, 다음 해에도 남아 있을 확률(**유지율**)이 $r$로 일정하며, 할인율이 $d$라면 $$CLV = m \times \frac{1 + d}{1 + d - r}$$ 이다(첫해 이익을 연초에 받는다고 가정한 형태). 할인을 무시하면($d = 0$) $CLV = \frac{m}{1 - r}$로, $\frac{1}{1-r}$이 **기대 관계 기간**이다. 유지율 80%면 평균 5년 관계다.

The key insight from CLV: **a small improvement in retention changes CLV greatly.** With no discounting and $m = 10$, a retention rate of 80% gives a CLV of 50, and 90% gives 100. A 10-percentage-point improvement in retention doubles customer value. That is why retaining existing customers (customer service, membership, quality) matters as much as acquiring new ones.

CLV is compared with the **customer acquisition cost** (CAC) to set the limit of marketing investment. CLV must be sufficiently larger than CAC (a target of 3 times or more is often mentioned) for acquiring customers to be profitable. Also, customers can be divided by CLV so that more retention effort is focused on high-value customers. However, treating customers differently because their CLV is low can raise fairness and reputation problems.

Limitations: actual retention rates are not constant (churn is often highest in the first year), and purchase amounts differ by customer. CLV is a **forecast**, so it changes greatly when assumptions change. In businesses that are not subscription-based (where customers do not announce they are leaving), it is hard even to define the retention rate. Do not trust CLV blindly as a single number; look at its sensitivity as well. This lesson is conceptual and is not advice on practical analysis.

mkt-17.title: A/B Testing: Causal Experiments in Marketing
explain: After a new webpage design was applied, sales rose. Was it thanks to the design? There may also have been a seasonal effect, a competitor's stockout, or an increase in advertising at the same time. A before-and-after comparison cannot sort out the cause. An **A/B test** is a **randomized controlled experiment** that randomly divides customers into two groups, applies a change to only one, and compares the results. Hypothesis testing from statistics is used in marketing as it is.

Design steps: (1) **Hypothesis**: "Changing the color of the purchase button raises the conversion rate." (2) **Metric**: decide in advance what will be used to judge success (conversion rate, average order value). (3) **Random assignment**: visitors are randomly assigned to A (existing) and B (new version). Because assignment is random, the two groups are on average the same in every other condition, so the difference can be attributed to the change. (4) **Sample size**: decide in advance enough visitors to detect the desired effect.

Analyzing results: test whether the difference in conversion rates between the two groups can be explained by chance. With conversion rates $p_A$, $p_B$ and group size $n$ each, the standard error of the difference is approximately $\sqrt{\frac{p_A(1-p_A)}{n} + \frac{p_B(1-p_B)}{n}}$, and if $z = \frac{p_B - p_A}{SE}$ is greater than 1.96, the result is significant at the 5% significance level. Along with significance, report the **effect size** and the **confidence interval**.

Common pitfalls: (1) **Peeking and stopping midway**: if you keep looking at results and stop the moment they become significant, the probability of a false discovery rises sharply. Decide the sample size in advance and run to the end. (2) **Reporting only the significant ones among many metrics** (multiple comparisons). (3) **Novelty effect**: at first the response is good because it is new, and it disappears over time. (4) **Sample contamination**: if the same person sees both versions, or there is interaction between groups (shared coupons), the comparison breaks down.

Limits and ethics: A/B tests are strong on short-term, measurable metrics but have difficulty capturing effects such as brand image or long-term loyalty. Also, price discrimination experiments and experiments with designs that manipulate users (dark patterns) raise issues of fairness and consumer protection. Experiments must be designed within principles that protect participants' rights and privacy.

mkt-18.title: Funnel Analysis and Marketing Performance Metrics
explain: To show whether marketing activity ultimately led to sales and profit, one must measure, stage by stage, the process by which customers go from awareness to purchase. The tool for that is **funnel** analysis. Looking at how many drop out at each stage shows where to fix.

explain.alt: Four funnel-shaped stages. Impressions 100,000 people, clicks 4,000 people, cart 800 people, purchase 200 people.

explain: The **conversion rate** at each stage is the proportion that moved on to the next stage. In the figure, impressions → clicks is 4% (**click-through rate**, CTR), clicks → cart is 20%, and cart → purchase is 25%. The **overall conversion rate** is the **product** of the stage conversion rates: $0.04 \times 0.20 \times 0.25 = 0.002$, that is, 0.2% of impressions. The fact that it is a product matters. Doubling the conversion rate at any stage doubles final purchases. The most efficient improvement point is the **stage with large room for improvement and low cost**.

Key performance metrics (in the formulas, 마케팅 비용 is marketing cost, 신규 고객 수 is number of new customers, 마케팅으로 늘어난 공헌이익 is contribution margin gained from marketing, 광고로 발생한 매출 is revenue generated by advertising, and 광고비 is advertising cost): **customer acquisition cost** $CAC = \frac{\text{마케팅 비용}}{\text{신규 고객 수}}$. **Marketing ROI** $= \frac{\text{마케팅으로 늘어난 공헌이익} - \text{마케팅 비용}}{\text{마케팅 비용}}$. **Return on ad spend** (ROAS) $= \frac{\text{광고로 발생한 매출}}{\text{광고비}}$. Caution: ROAS is based on revenue and ignores cost. Even with a ROAS of 300%, if the contribution margin rate is 25%, the profit is smaller than the advertising cost.

Principles for using metrics: look at **actionable metrics** (conversion rate, retention rate, CLV/CAC) rather than **vanity metrics** (views and follower counts, which look big but are weakly tied to business results). Optimizing stage metrics separately can make the whole worse. If provocative ads are used just to raise the click-through rate, clicks rise but the conversion rate afterward falls. Judge by the whole funnel and final profit.

Limitations: a funnel simplifies the customer journey into a straight line. Real customers skip stages or go back. Also, whether a change in a stage's conversion rate is due to marketing or to other factors must be confirmed with experiments (the previous lesson). This lesson is conceptual and is not advice on evaluating practical performance.

mkt-19.title: Integrated Problem Solving: Validating the STP, Price, and CLV of a Fictional New Product
explain: The first capstone lesson validates the plan for one fictional new product in turn with the tools from Stages 2 to 5. Situation: a startup is preparing a "lunch salad subscription" service for office workers. Delivery three times a week, a monthly subscription. All figures are fictional.

**Stage 1 (STP and positioning)**: In segmentation research, the segment of office workers with "high health interest and little lunch time" fits as the target. On the competitive map (price × health image), convenience-store salads are "low price, medium health" and premium salad specialty shops are "high price, high health." The point of difference is "specialty-shop level health + the convenience of regular delivery." The points of parity are hygiene certification and a freshness guarantee.

**Stage 2 (price)**: The target customer's current alternative is eating out for lunch at an average of 10,000 won × 12 times a month = 120,000 won (reference value). If the value of saved travel and waiting time is estimated at 30,000 won a month, EVC = 150,000 won. If the monthly subscription fee is set at 119,000 won, the customer's gain is sufficient, and the reference price comparison that "it is cheaper than eating out" (prospect theory) can also be used. If the cost per meal is 6,500 won, the monthly cost is 78,000 won and the contribution margin is about 41,000 won.

**Stage 3 (CLV and acquisition cost)**: Assuming a monthly retention rate of 85% (ignoring discounting), $CLV = 4.1/(1 - 0.85) \approx 27.3$ (in units of 10,000 won), that is, about 273,000 won. The expected subscription duration is about 6.7 months. The customer acquisition cost target is at most about 90,000 won, one third of CLV. Estimate the conversion rate at each stage of the funnel (ad impression → trial signup → first subscription → retention for 2 months) to check whether this CAC is feasible.

**Stage 4 (channels and IMC)**: A company-wide group subscription (B2B) channel wins many customers with a single sales effort, lowering CAC. For individual customers: social media ads (awareness) → free trial (promotion) → in-office referral program (reference group influence). The message is unified across all channels as "a healthy lunch for busy office workers."

**Critique**: The 85% retention rate is the most sensitive assumption. At 75%, CLV falls 40% to about 164,000 won, and the CAC target also falls to 55,000 won. Actual retention in the first three months should be confirmed while improving it with A/B tests (menu variety, a pause function). Raw material price increases or higher delivery costs reduce the contribution margin, so look at them in scenarios as well.

mkt-20.title: Bachelor's Capstone: An Integrated Marketing Plan for a New Product
explain: The final task is to **choose one fictional new product (or service), write an integrated marketing plan, and critique the methods for validating its key assumptions with metrics and its risks**. It is not a plan for any real company or product, and it is not advice on advertising law or practical execution.

Plan framework: (1) **Market and customer understanding**: target segment, the customer's involvement and purchase decision process, reference groups. (2) **Positioning**: frame of reference, points of parity, points of difference, position on the positioning map. (3) **Price**: value-based rationale (EVC), elasticity estimate, psychological pricing tactics and their ethical limits. (4) **Distribution**: channel composition and omnichannel experience, channel conflict management. (5) **Communication**: IMC message, means for each stage of the customer journey, reach and frequency targets. (6) **Profitability validation**: contribution margin, CLV, CAC, working backward through the funnel. (7) **Measurement and experiments**: key metrics, an A/B test plan. (8) **Risks and critique**: the most sensitive assumption, failure scenarios, consumer protection and ethics.

Features of a good plan: every element **points to the same positioning** (a premium positioning with constant discount promotions is a contradiction). Numbers are written with their basis, and the most uncertain assumption is presented together with a **validation plan**. Tactics that deceive or manipulate customers (false list prices, dark patterns) are not used.
This task is not graded. The text you submit is saved only on this device, and you can view it again under 'My Writing' in 'My Progress'.
